Empirical Research Plan  
“TARP Capital Injections and Mortgage-Lending Risk”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Preferred design: Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with matched control banks, augmented with an event-study (dynamic DiD).

Rationale  
• Treatment—the receipt of TARP capital—occurs at a clearly observed date (first disbursement to each bank).  
• We observe multiple years of pre- and post-treatment loan-level outcomes.  
• Non-recipient banks that applied for TARP provide a natural comparison group: they faced the same crisis, voluntarily revealed information to regulators, but did not receive the capital injection.  
• Combining propensity-score matching (to improve covariate balance) with DiD (to difference out time-invariant unobservables) delivers a credible counterfactual.  
• The dynamic event-study checks the common-trend assumption and allows flexible treatment timing (some banks received funds in 2009).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 if bank i received any CPP capital between Oct-2008 and Dec-2009; 0 otherwise.

Treatment timing  
bank-specific Post_it = 1 for all quarters (or years) ≥ the calendar quarter in which bank i first received CPP funds; 0 beforehand.

Control group  
Banks that (i) applied for CPP but never received funds and (ii) are matched to treated banks on 2007 balance-sheet characteristics (size, tier-1 ratio, NPL ratio, profitability, state location). Matching is done by propensity score with caliper 0.05 and without replacement.

Unit of observation  
Loan-level (preferred) or bank-year aggregates (robustness). The DiD term is Treated_i × Post_it.

Outcome variables (risk proxies)  
• High-LTV dummy (LTV ≥ 90)  
• Loan-to-Income ratio  
• Applicant income (inverse measure of risk)  
• Denial rate (bank-level)  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: Absent CPP capital, risk measures at treated and control banks would have evolved in parallel.  
Plausibility: Banks applied voluntarily and faced the same macro shock; matching further aligns fundamentals. We will test for pre-trend equality in 2006-2007.

A2. No differential shocks coincident with treatment: No other policy hit treated banks right at the disbursement date.  
Plausibility: Other crisis programs (e.g., FDIC TLGP) applied almost universally and are absorbed by year fixed effects.

A3. Stable composition: Treated and control groups do not change systematically via mergers or failures that correlate with treatment.  
Plausibility: Some failures occurred; we will drop banks that exited before 2010 and show robustness to their inclusion.

A4. SUTVA: Each bank’s treatment status does not affect the counterfactual risk-taking of other banks (no spillovers).  
Plausibility: Geographic lending markets overlap, so we will probe for spillovers in county-level regressions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Selection on unobservables (regulators preferred “healthier” applicants).  
Mitigation:  
• Bank fixed effects difference out all time-invariant traits, observed or not.  
• Event-study graph: flat pre-period implies limited selection on differential trends.  
• IV robustness: use regulator workload shocks (e.g., regional Fed Reserve CPP review load) as an instrument for actual receipt.

T2. Macro housing-market heterogeneity. If treated banks lend in faster-collapsing housing markets, risk may mechanically rise.  
Mitigation: Include county-year fixed effects (loan-level specs) or bank × state housing price index interactions.

T3. Measurement error in risk proxies (esp. LTV reported in HMDA).  
Mitigation: Focus on “high-LTV” indicator (less noisy), winsorise continuous variables, replicate results with alternative proxies (e.g., share of FHA/VA loans).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(MatchIt)
library(fixest)        # fast fe regressions
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load Data ----------------------------------------------------
hmda <- fread("hmda_2006_2010.csv")       # loan-level
tarp <- fread("tarp_transactions.csv")    # bank_id, date_received
y9c  <- fread("fr_y9c_2005_2010.csv")     # bank-year financials
apps <- fread("tarp_applications.csv")    # applicants universe

# 2. Construct Bank-level Treatment ------------------------------
tarp[, treated := 1]
tarp[, treat_date := as.Date(date_received)]
first_tarp <- tarp[, .(treat_date = min(treat_date)), by = bank_id]

# merge applicants to add zeros
banks <- merge(apps, first_tarp, by = "bank_id", all.x = TRUE)
banks[is.na(treated), treated := 0]

# 3. Propensity Score Matching (based on 2007 financials) ---------
base07 <- y9c[year == 2007]
ps_data <- merge(banks, base07, by = "bank_id")
m.out <- matchit(treated ~ log(total_assets) + tier1_ratio + npl_ratio +
                   roa, data = ps_data, method = "nearest", caliper = 0.05)
matched_ids <- data.table(bank_id = ps_data$bank_id)[m.out$match.matrix]

# keep matched sample
banks_matched <- banks[bank_id %in% matched_ids$bank_id]

# 4. Merge Loan-level Data & Create DiD Variables -----------------
dd <- merge(hmda, banks_matched[, .(bank_id, treated, treat_date)],
            by = "bank_id")

dd[, year := as.integer(substr(action_date, 1, 4))]
dd[, post := ifelse(!is.na(treat_date) & action_date >= treat_date, 1, 0)]
dd[, did := treated * post]

# outcome: high LTV
dd[, high_ltv := as.integer(ltv >= 90)]

# 5. Main DiD Regression -----------------------------------------
est1 <- feols(high_ltv ~ did + bank_fe + i(year), 
              cluster = ~bank_id, data = dd,
              fixef = ~bank_id + year)
summary(est1)

# 6. Event-Study (Sun & Abraham style) ---------------------------
dd[, rel_year := year - year(treat_date)]
dd[treated == 0, rel_year := -99] # control group
est2 <- feols(high_ltv ~ sunab(rel_year, treated) | bank_id + year,
              cluster = ~bank_id, data = dd)
iplot(est2)   # pre-trend visual

# 7. Robustness: Bank-Year Aggregates & Alt Outcome --------------
bank_year <- dd[, .(
  share_high_ltv = mean(high_ltv),
  avg_lti = mean(lti, na.rm = TRUE)
), by = .(bank_id, year, treated, post)]

robust <- feols(share_high_ltv ~ treated*post | bank_id + year,
                cluster = ~bank_id, data = bank_year)
summary(robust)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory is ambiguous. Political pressure (“lend more”) pushes toward volume, perhaps lowering risk screens, while improved capitalization could make banks safer and thus more willing to originate riskier loans (moral hazard). My prior: Treated banks will increase the share of high-risk mortgages by 2-4 pp relative to controls (≈10–20 % of the pre-crisis mean share of ~20 %).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = weak)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Clear treatment date & variation .............. 1  
2. Overlap / common support after matching ....... 0.9  
3. Parallel pre-trends (based on tests) .......... 0.8  
4. No simultaneity / confounding shocks .......... 0.7  
5. Robust standard errors & clustering ........... 1  

Total (avg) ...................................... 0.88  

Overall, with extensive pre-trend diagnostics, alternative control groups, and event-study confirmation, the design should deliver credible causal estimates of how TARP capital influenced banks’ mortgage-lending risk.
